# Dynamic UI

## Comparing priors

Our Beta-Binomial app has a single prior. To see how much the posterior depends on that choice we want to compare several priors, without knowing in advance how many there will be.

![](imgs/Lec23_app.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}


## A card for each prior

Each prior needs its own pair of inputs and every input needs its own id. A function that builds the ids from a number lets us make as many cards as we need.

::: {.small}
```r
prior_card = function(id) {
  card(
    card_header(paste("Prior", id)),
    numericInput(paste0("a_", id), "Prior # of heads", min = 0, value = 1),
    numericInput(paste0("b_", id), "Prior # of tails", min = 0, value = 1)
  )
}
```
:::

`prior_card(2)` creates the inputs `a_2` and `b_2`, which the server reads as `input$a_2` and `input$b_2`.


## A first attempt with `renderUI()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%' .small}
```r
sidebar(
  ...,
  actionButton("add", "Add prior"),
  uiOutput("priors")
)
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%' .small}
```r
output$priors = renderUI({
  map(
    seq_len(input$add), prior_card
  )
})
```
:::
::::

::: {.medium}
* `input$add` counts clicks, so each click rebuilds the output with one more card.

* Rebuilding replaces all of the cards, including the ones already on the page, so every input goes back to its default value.

* The cards are always `1` to `input$add`, which leaves no way to remove one from the middle.
:::


## `insertUI()` & `removeUI()`

These functions add and remove pieces of UI from the server without touching anything else on the page.

::: {.small}
```r
insertUI(selector = "#priors", where = "beforeEnd", ui = prior_card(1))
```

```r
removeUI(selector = "#prior_1")
```
:::

::: {.medium}
* `selector` is a CSS selector, as used with `rvest`. `#priors` matches the element whose id is `priors`, so the UI needs one, e.g. an empty `div(id = "priors")`.

* `where` places the new UI relative to the selected element. `beforeEnd` makes it the last child, `afterBegin` the first, and `beforeBegin` and `afterEnd` put it outside the element.

* Both are side effects, so they are called from an observer and never from a `render*()` function or a reactive.
:::


## Adding a prior

::: {.small}
```r
ids = reactiveVal(integer())

observe({
  id = input$add

  insertUI("#priors", where = "beforeEnd", ui = prior_card(id))
  ids(c(ids(), id))
}) |>
  bindEvent(input$add)
```
:::

::: {.medium}
* The click count is different for every click, which makes it a convenient source of unique ids.

* `reactiveVal()` creates a reactive value that we set ourselves. `ids()` reads it and `ids(x)` replaces it, which invalidates anything that has read it.

* The server has no other record of what is on the page, so `ids` is how the rest of the app knows which priors exist.
:::


## Removing a prior

Each card gets an id, a button, and its own observer.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width='50%' .small}
```r
card(
  id = paste0("prior_", id),
  card_header(
    paste("Prior", id),
    actionButton(
      paste0("remove_", id), NULL,
      icon = icon("xmark")
    )
  ),
  ...
)
```
:::

::: {.column width='50%' .small}
```r
observe({
  removeUI(paste0("#prior_", id))
  ids(setdiff(ids(), id))
}) |>
  bindEvent(
    input[[paste0("remove_", id)]],
    once = TRUE
  )
```
:::
::::

::: {.medium}
* The observer is created inside the observer for `input$add`, where `id` is known. `once = TRUE` destroys it after it has run.

* `removeUI()` only removes the HTML. `input$a_2` keeps its last value, so it is `ids()` that tells us which priors are left.
:::


## Reading the inputs

The ids are built at run time, so inputs are read with `input[[...]]`. A new card's inputs start as `NULL`, hence the `req()`.

::: {.xsmall}
```r
d = reactive({
  map(
    ids(),
    \(id) {
      a = input[[paste0("a_", id)]]
      b = input[[paste0("b_", id)]]
      req(a, b)

      tibble(
        prior = paste("Prior", id),
        p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 501),
        density = dbeta(p, a + input$x, b + input$n - input$x)
      )
    }
  ) |>
    list_rbind()
})
```
:::


## Example

Build a version of the Beta-Binomial app that plots the posterior for any number of priors, with buttons to add and remove them.


## What we ended up with

The app works, but the code for a single card is hard to follow and harder to reuse.

* The naming scheme (`prior_1`, `a_1`, `b_1`, `remove_1`) is repeated by hand in the UI function, both observers, and the reactive.

* The logic for one card is spread over four separate places in the app.

* Every id lives in one shared namespace, so nothing stops another part of the app from also using `a_1`.

* Using the cards in a second app means copying all of these pieces and keeping them in sync.


# Modules

## Shiny modules

A module is a pair of functions that together describe one piece of an app, such as a single prior card.

* The module UI function takes an `id` and returns UI, like `prior_card()` did.

* The module server function takes the same `id` and holds the server code for that UI.

* Everything inside the module is namespaced by the `id`. The module's code refers to `input$a`, while the rest of the app sees that input as `prior_1-a`.

A module can then be used several times in one app, each time with a different `id`, without any of the copies interfering with each other.


## `NS()`

Namespacing is nothing more than a prefix on the id. `NS()` returns a function that adds the prefix.

::: {.small}
```{r ns}
ns = NS("prior_1")
```

```{r ns-use}
ns("a")
ns("remove")
```
:::

A module UI function wraps every input and output id in `ns()`. Leaving one out is the most common mistake with modules. The app still runs, but the module's server never sees that input.


## Module UI

By convention the function is named `*_ui()` and `id` is its first argument. Other arguments, like `label` here, are up to us.

::: {.small}
```r
prior_ui = function(id, label) {
  ns = NS(id)

  card(
    id = ns("card"),
    card_header(
      label,
      actionButton(ns("remove"), NULL, icon = icon("xmark"))
    ),
    numericInput(ns("a"), "Prior # of heads", min = 0, value = 1),
    numericInput(ns("b"), "Prior # of tails", min = 0, value = 1)
  )
}
```
:::


## Module server

::: {.small}
```r
prior_server = function(id, label, x, n) {
  moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    reactive({
      req(input$a, input$b)

      tibble(
        prior = label,
        p = seq(0, 1, length.out = 501),
        density = dbeta(p, input$a + x(), input$b + n() - x())
      )
    })
  })
}
```
:::

::: {.medium}
* The app's `input$x` is not visible here. Anything the module needs is passed in as a reactive and read as `x()`.

* The inner function's value is returned to the caller.
:::


## Using a module

Call each function once per copy, with matching ids.

::: {.xsmall}
```r
ui = page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    ...,
    prior_ui("prior_1", "Prior 1"),
    prior_ui("prior_2", "Prior 2")
  ),
  plotOutput("plot")
)

server = function(input, output, session) {
  x = reactive(input$x)
  n = reactive(input$n)
  prior_1 = prior_server("prior_1", "Prior 1", x, n)
  prior_2 = prior_server("prior_2", "Prior 2", x, n)

  d = reactive(bind_rows(prior_1(), prior_2()))
  ...
}
```
:::


## Modules & dynamic UI

A module server can be started at any time. Each click inserts a new copy of the UI and starts its server.

::: {.xsmall}
```r
priors = reactiveVal(list())

observe({
  id = paste0("prior_", input$add)
  label = paste("Prior", input$add)

  insertUI("#priors", where = "beforeEnd", ui = prior_ui(id, label))
  prior = prior_server(id, label, x = reactive(input$x), n = reactive(input$n))
  priors(c(priors(), prior))
}) |>
  bindEvent(input$add)

d = reactive({
  map(priors(), \(prior) prior()) |>
    list_rbind()
})
```
:::


## A module that removes itself

::: {.xsmall}
```r
moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
  removed = reactiveVal(FALSE)

  observe({
    removeUI(paste0("#", session$ns("card")))
    removed(TRUE)
  }) |>
    bindEvent(input$remove, once = TRUE)

  reactive({
    if (removed()) return(NULL)
    ...
  })
})
```
:::

::: {.medium}
* `input$remove` is namespaced for us but a CSS selector is not. `session$ns()` is the module's own `NS()` function, which gives the full id of the card.

* Shiny cannot shut down a module's server. After removal its reactive stays in `priors()` and returns `NULL`, which `list_rbind()` drops.
:::


## Example

Rewrite the prior comparison app so that each prior card is a module.


## Working with modules

::: {.medium}
* Name the pair `*_ui()` and `*_server()`, and keep the two functions together. Files in an app's `R/` folder are sourced automatically, so `R/prior.R` is a good home for them.

* Pass reactives into a module without calling them, as `x = reactive(input$x)` or `x = d`. Passing `input$x` hands over a single value that never updates.

* Return a reactive, or a list of reactives, for anything the rest of the app needs. Avoid reaching into a module's inputs from outside via `input[["prior_1-a"]]`.

* Modules can contain other modules. Inside a module the ids are relative, so a nested module is called with a plain id in the server and with `ns("id")` in the UI.

* A module server can be tested without a browser using `testServer()`.
:::


# Summary {visibility="uncounted"}

## Takeaways {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.medium}
* `renderUI()` rebuilds everything it returns, which resets any inputs it contains. `insertUI()` and `removeUI()` change one piece of the page and leave the rest alone.

* UI that is added while the app runs needs unique ids and a record on the server of what currently exists, typically kept in a `reactiveVal()`. Inputs with generated ids are read with `input[[id]]`.

* Doing this by pasting ids together works, but the naming scheme ends up repeated throughout the app.

* A module pairs a UI function with a server function that share an `id`. `NS()` prefixes the ids in the UI and `moduleServer()` gives the server a view of only its own inputs and outputs.

* Reactives go into a module as arguments and come out as its return value.

* Module servers can be started from an observer, which makes modules a good fit for UI that is created on demand.
:::
